title: ANI v. OpenAI — first Indian judicial ruling on AI training
detail: ANI (Asian News International) sued OpenAI in November 2024, alleging OpenAI used ANI's news reports without permission to train ChatGPT, and separately that ChatGPT fabricated stories attributed to ANI. The Digital News Publishers Association and the Federation of Indian Publishers intervened. The Delhi High Court refused the interim injunction; the suit continues to trial on the merits.
status: interim — injunction refused, suit continues to trial
action: Treat the outcome as favourable but provisional: build on it, do not bet the corpus architecture on it surviving trial or appeal.
source: Delhi High Court, Justice Amit Bansal, judgment 24 July 2026, 135 pages (§14.1)
note: §14 opens: "This section changed materially four days before this document was written." §A.7 grades the ruling high confidence — "multiple independent legal and business outlets" — and §20 lists the coverage as Business Standard, LawBeat, The New Publishing Standard. The document cites no case number or neutral citation.

title: Training held prima facie fair dealing for research
detail: OpenAI's storage and use of ANI's content to train its models is prima facie protected as "fair dealing" for "private or personal use, including research".
status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
action: You may rely on it as the current Indian position on ingestion for training, while keeping the corpus decomposable in case it is re-examined.
source: Section 52(1)(a)(i) of the Copyright Act, 1957, as applied in ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)
note: §14.1 also states this stretch of Section 52(1)(a)(i) "is the entire legal foundation" for training in India — see L12.

title: ANI failed to establish memorisation or reproduction
detail: ANI failed to establish that ChatGPT memorised or reproduced its copyrighted news reports.
status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
action: Run and document memorisation testing so you can affirmatively demonstrate low memorisation — see L26.
source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

title: Copyright protects expression, not facts
detail: Copyright protects expression, not the underlying facts or information — "news of the day" is not protected.
status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

title: Commercial entities not automatically excluded from fair dealing
detail: The court rejected the argument that commercial entities are automatically excluded from claiming the fair-dealing defence.
status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)
note: Commentary summarised in the document treats this as one of the ruling's vulnerabilities on appeal — see L08.

title: Practical effect — evidentiary burden shifts to publishers
detail: The burden has shifted onto publishers to prove memorisation or reproduction, not merely ingestion — a considerably harder evidentiary bar. For an India-based project this is a meaningfully favourable environment relative to 12 months ago. "It is not a licence to scrape indiscriminately."
action: Do not read the ruling as permission to scrape; keep the risk-tiered corpus and compliance gate regardless.
source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

title: Limit 1 — these are prima facie findings
detail: The judgment expressly states the findings do not control the final outcome. Discovery, expert evidence and trial are still ahead.
action: Do not architect anything that only works if these findings hold.
source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 1

title: Limit 2 — single-judge interim order, appealable
detail: It is a single-judge interim order; an appellate bench could land differently. Serious commentary has already identified vulnerabilities: that the court treated an internal technical process as "private use" even where the objective purpose is a public commercial product; that it applied Canadian "research" jurisprudence to differently-worded Indian text; and that it arguably used updating construction to create a commercial AI-training exception that Parliament did not enact.
action: Keep the clean tier separable so a compliant base model can be retrained if the ruling is reversed on appeal.
source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 2; mitigation in §18.2
note: The document names no commentator or publication for the "serious commentary".

title: Limit 3 — the hallucination / false-attribution claim is unresolved
detail: ANI's suit always had two limbs; only the training limb was addressed. The hallucination/false-attribution claim remains unresolved.
source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 3
note: This is item 3 of the document's own five-item list. The document does not state which regime the false-attribution limb sounds in (passing off, defamation, or otherwise).

title: Limit 4 — it does not override contracts
detail: A NonCommercial licence (NCERT, DIKSHA, NPTEL) is a contract, not a copyright default. Fair dealing does not let you ignore it.
action: Exclude NC-licensed corpora from a commercial model, or licence them — see L31 and L28.
source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 4

title: Limit 5 — it does not touch the DPDP Act
detail: Copyright and data protection are separate regimes; the ruling says nothing about DPDP obligations.
action: Run the DPDP compliance programme independently of any copyright analysis.
source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 5
note: §14.2 adds that for an India-based training run "data protection is a bigger operational constraint than copyright".

title: India has no explicit TDM exception — the statute was stretched
detail: Unlike the EU (DSM Directive Arts. 3–4) or Japan (Art. 30-4), Indian copyright law is right-holder-centric with a closed list of fair-dealing purposes. The ANI ruling stretched Section 52(1)(a)(i) to cover training. "That stretch is the entire legal foundation, and it is one appeal away from re-examination."
status: no statutory TDM exception; judicial stretch only
action: Assume the foundation can move; keep the corpus decomposable and the clean tier trainable on its own.
source: §14.1, closing paragraph (Copyright Act 1957 s.52(1)(a)(i); EU DSM Directive Arts. 3–4; Japan Art. 30-4)
note: This point sits in its own paragraph in §14.1, outside the numbered five-item "What it does NOT mean" list — so the document actually states six distinct limits on the ruling, not five.

title: You are a Data Fiduciary
detail: You determine the purpose and means of processing training data, so you are a Data Fiduciary. Obligations attach even when data comes from third parties or is processed on external infrastructure.
action: Accept Data Fiduciary duties for the whole pipeline, including third-party corpora and external compute.
source: DPDP Act 2023 + DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
note: §14.2 frames the whole regime: "For an India-based training run, data protection is a bigger operational constraint than copyright."

title: Consent-centric processing
detail: Free, specific, informed consent per specified purpose; notices must itemise the personal data collected and the exact purpose.
action: Itemise personal data and purpose in the notice; do not rely on generic blanket consent.
source: DPDP Act 2023 + DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
note: The document does not state how consent is to be obtained for web-scraped personal data — that gap is what makes the "publicly available" exemption (L16) load-bearing.

title: Erasure obligation — implies selective removal and arguably unlearning
detail: Data must be erased when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is served. This implies the ability to selectively remove data from training pipelines and logs — and, arguably, to handle machine unlearning. Requests must be addressed within 90 days.
action: Build an erasure-request index (document hash → shard → checkpoint lineage) on day one; retrofitting provenance into a 15T-token corpus is effectively impossible.
source: DPDP Act 2023; 90-day deadline at Rule 14, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
note: The document says machine unlearning is "arguably" required — it does not claim the Act or Rules mandate it expressly.

title: "Publicly available" exemption — scope contested
detail: Section 3(c)(ii) excludes personal data the data principal made publicly available, but the scope is contested. MeitY stated in the Rajya Sabha (Aug 2024) that scraping publicly available user data remains subject to the IT Act, IT Rules and DPDP Act including consent and transparency obligations — which "sits uneasily with the plain text". IAMAI formally petitioned MeitY in August 2025 seeking an explicit AI-training exemption under Section 17(5). As of this writing, no such blanket exemption has been notified.
status: contested — no exemption notified as of 28 July 2026
action: Do not treat "it was public" as a complete answer; keep consent and transparency obligations live for scraped personal data.
source: DPDP Act 2023 s.3(c)(ii); MeitY statement in the Rajya Sabha, Aug 2024; IAMAI petition to MeitY, Aug 2025 seeking s.17(5) exemption (§14.2)

title: Research exemption is purpose-based and may not cover commercial training
detail: Section 17(2)(b) conditionally exempts research processing — but exemptions are purpose-based, and commercial model training is not obviously research.
action: Do not plan on the research exemption for a commercial training run.
note: Recorded as a limit rather than an obligation: it constrains a defence, it does not impose a duty. Note the tension with the copyright side, where the ANI ruling accepted training as "research" under the Copyright Act (L02) — the document does not reconcile the two.

title: Children's data — verifiable parental consent, no profiling
detail: Verifiable parental consent is required for under-18s; no tracking, profiling, or behavioural targeting of children. "For a model trained on educational content this is directly relevant."
action: Add children's-data detection and exclusion to the ingestion gate.
source: DPDP Act 2023 s.9 / Rule 10, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)

title: Cross-border transfer restricted to notified countries
detail: Transfers are permitted to notified countries. Relevant if you train on non-Indian cloud.
action: Check the notified-country list before choosing non-Indian training infrastructure.
source: DPDP Act 2023 s.16 / Rule 15, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
note: The document does not say which countries are notified.

title: Ingestion gate — PII and India-specific ID detection
detail: The ingestion gate must do PII detection and redaction (names, phones, emails, addresses), India-specific ID pattern detection (Aadhaar, PAN, passport, voter ID, bank), and children's-data detection and exclusion.
action: Build automated Aadhaar/PAN/passport-pattern detectors into ingestion; redact PII and exclude children's data before anything reaches the corpus.
source: §14.2 "Operational requirements this imposes on your pipeline"; §13.4 ("Any government/personal/financial identity documents"); §17 SAFETY & COMPLIANCE GATE
note: The §17 pipeline diagram restates the same gate: "PII redaction · Aadhaar/PAN/passport/bank pattern detection", CSAM hash matching, toxicity, children's-data exclusion, licence tag propagation.

title: Provenance record per document
detail: Keep a provenance record for every document: source URL, licence, retrieval date, hash.
action: Emit a per-document provenance record at ingestion; do not defer it.
source: §14.2 operational-requirements block; §17 SAFETY & COMPLIANCE GATE

title: Erasure-request index (hash → shard → checkpoint lineage)
detail: Maintain an erasure-request index mapping document hash → shard → checkpoint lineage. "The erasure-request index is the part teams skip and later regret. Build it on day one; retrofitting provenance into a 15T-token corpus is effectively impossible."
action: Build the index before the first large ingestion run.
source: §14.2 operational-requirements block; mitigation repeated in §18.2 ("DPDP erasure request against training data")

title: Posture 1 — tier the corpus by risk and prove the clean tier first
detail: Tier your corpus by risk exactly as this document does: build the clean tier first and prove the model works on it.
action: Build and validate on the clean tier before touching restricted material.
source: §14.3 "A defensible legal posture (not legal advice)", item 1

title: Posture 2 — honour robots.txt, noai/noimageai, and TDM reservation signals
detail: Honour robots.txt, `noai`/`noimageai` meta tags, and TDM reservation signals. "Even without a statutory obligation, ignoring them converts an arguable case into a wilful one."
action: Enforce the signals at fetch time in the acquisition stage.
source: §14.3 item 2; restated in the §17 ACQUISITION block ("robots.txt + noai + TDM-reservation honoured at fetch time")

title: Posture 3 — publish a data statement
detail: Publish a data statement covering sources, licences, filtering, and an opt-out mechanism. Dolma and Common Corpus are the models to copy. "Transparency is a legal asset, not a liability."
action: Publish the data statement alongside the model.
source: §14.3 item 3

title: Posture 4 — run and document memorisation testing
detail: Run and document memorisation testing. The ANI ruling turned on ANI's failure to prove memorisation, so being able to affirmatively demonstrate low memorisation "is now a defensive asset with judicial backing".
status: recommended — now an affirmative legal asset in India
action: Run memorisation tests and publish the results.
source: §14.3 item 4; repeated as the §18.2 mitigation for "Model memorises and regurgitates Indic news"

title: Posture 5 — maintain a takedown/opt-out channel and act on it
detail: Maintain a takedown/opt-out channel and act on it.
action: Stand up the channel and process requests.
source: §14.3 item 5
note: The document gives no SLA for this channel; the only stated deadline is the 90-day DPDP erasure window in L15.

title: Posture 6 — get NCERT/MoE and BharatGen licences in writing
detail: Get NCERT/MoE and BharatGen licences in writing. "Two letters could be worth more than a trillion scraped tokens."
action: Pursue written licences from NCERT/MoE and BharatGen.
source: §14.3 item 6
note: §13.2 adds the specific asks: an MoU for Bharat Data Sagar, and the exact EKA licence string in writing.

title: Keep the clean tier separable against an appeal reversal
detail: Mitigation for the risk "ANI ruling reversed on appeal": keep the clean tier separable so you can retrain a compliant base if needed. "Do not architect a corpus you cannot decompose."
action: Keep the corpus decomposable by licence/risk tier so a compliant base can be retrained.
source: §18.2 Legal and reputational risks

title: Hard-fail the build on any NonCommercial licence tag
detail: Mitigation for "NC-licensed content leaks into the mix": automated licence-tag propagation, and hard-fail the build on any NC tag, not a warning.
action: Propagate licence tags through the pipeline and fail the build (not warn) on any NC tag.
source: §18.2 Legal and reputational risks
note: §18.2 adds a related supply-chain rule for synthetic data: prefer Apache-2.0 generators (Qwen3, some Nemotron) for anything that will be redistributed, to avoid Gemma/Llama/Qwen licence-chain terms.

title: NonCommercial-licensed datasets — exclude from a commercial model
detail: Named NC datasets: NCERT textbooks / DIKSHA textbook content (CC BY-NC-ND, NCERT/MoE, K-12 curriculum in 36 languages — NC and ND); DIKSHA non-textbook resources (CC BY-NC-SA); NPTEL / SWAYAM course content (typically CC BY-NC-SA, MoE/IITs/IISc, 2,500+ courses); AI4Bharat IndicNLP Corpus v1 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 2.7B words, 10 languages — IndicCorp v2 and Sangraha are NOT NC, only v1 is); NLLB mined bitext (CC BY-NC, Meta); ILDC Indian Legal Documents Corpus (research/non-commercial by request, Malik et al., 35K SC cases); xLAM some releases (CC BY-NC, Salesforce).
status: in force — exclusion or licence required
action: Exclude from a commercial model unless licensed; verify the specific xLAM release before use.
source: §13.1 ("Everything in this section requires either a licence, a legal sign-off, or exclusion")
note: §A.7 confirms NCERT CC BY-NC-ND and DIKSHA CC BY-NC-SA from NCERT/CIET's own site (high confidence). L10 explains why the ANI ruling does not help here.

title: BharatGen non-commercial model licence blocks distillation
detail: BharatGen Param-2 / Patram post-trained checkpoints carry a BharatGen non-commercial licence. These are models, not data — but the licence blocks distillation-based data generation.
action: Do not generate training data by distilling BharatGen checkpoints without a licence.

title: Bespoke / custom licences requiring negotiation
detail: BhashaKritika, 540B synthetic Indic tokens, Krutrim Community License (Krutrim AI Labs / Ola) — negotiate or replicate. Chitrakshara-IL / Chitrakshara-Cap, Krutrim licence — the largest Indic interleaved multimodal corpus. Bharat Data Sagar (BharatGen consortium) — not distributed; pursue an MoU; ₹1,293 crore of public investment, ~20T tokens claimed.
action: Negotiate, replicate, or pursue an MoU before planning around any of these.
note: §18.3 flags the 20T Bharat Data Sagar figure as unaudited; §A.7 grades it low confidence — "a CEO statement... Do not build a plan that depends on this being true."

title: The Stack v2 — OpenRAIL-M, per-file licences, and a live opt-out list
detail: The Stack v2 / StarCoder2 (BigCode / Software Heritage) is under BigCode OpenRAIL-M v1 plus per-file licences plus a live opt-out list.
action: Ingest the opt-out list and use the permissive-only subset.
note: The opt-out list is live, so it must be re-ingested, not snapshotted once — the document says "ingest the opt-out list" without stating a refresh cadence.

title: AIKosh — per-dataset licence ingestion required
detail: AIKosh datasets carry per-dataset licences: open, registered, or restricted, from various contributors via IndiaAI.
action: Ingest and enforce the licence per dataset rather than treating AIKosh as one licence.

title: ULCA / Bhashini — record-level attribution
detail: ULCA / Bhashini datasets are licensed per contributor with record-level attribution (Bhashini DIBD, MeitY).
action: Maintain an attribution manifest at record level.

title: EKA Pre-training Indic Corpus v1 — licence string unspecified
detail: The EKA Pre-training Indic Corpus v1 (Soket AI Labs + IIT Gandhinagar) is described only as "Open Source" — the licence string is unspecified.
action: Get the exact licence in writing before ingesting.
source: §13.2; repeated in §18.3 Honest unknowns ("EKA corpus licence string is unspecified. Get it in writing.")

title: Share-alike (copyleft) sources — attribution plus share-alike
detail: Wikipedia / Wikisource / Wikibooks / FineWiki (CC BY-SA), FLORES-200 (CC BY-SA 4.0) and People's Speech (CC BY-SA) are usable but carry attribution and share-alike obligations.
action: Attribute, and document your share-alike position.

title: Whether model weights are a derivative work of CC BY-SA data is unresolved
detail: Whether model weights are a "derivative work" of CC BY-SA training data is legally unresolved. "Most labs proceed; document your position."
action: Take and document an explicit position rather than leaving it implicit.
source: §13.3; §18.3 Honest unknowns ("unresolved anywhere in the world")

title: Stack Exchange / Stack Overflow — free bulk use is contested
detail: Stack Exchange / Stack Overflow dumps are CC BY-SA, but Stack Overflow now licenses data commercially to AI firms, so free bulk use is contested.
note: The document says "contested" without stating who is asserting what, or whether the CC BY-SA dump licence has actually been withdrawn.

title: Common Crawl carries third-party copyrighted content
detail: Common Crawl WET/WARC is distributed under CC BY (Common Crawl's own terms) but contains third-party copyrighted content. "The fair-dealing question in §14 lives here."
status: in force — the exposure the ANI ruling addresses
note: This is the direct link between the §13 corpus list and the §14 fair-dealing analysis: the CC licence covers the packaging, not the underlying pages.

title: Absolute blocklist — pirated and litigation-tainted book corpora
detail: Books3: pirated books via the Bibliotek torrent, core to Kadrey v. Meta; the original Pile download URL has been dead since ~Sept 2023. LibGen / Library Genesis: pirated, central to Tremblay v. OpenAI allegations. Anna's Archive / Z-Library: pirated shadow libraries.
action: Never ingest these; if you ingest The Pile, strip Books3 first.
source: §13.4 (cases named: Kadrey v. Meta; Tremblay v. OpenAI)
note: The document names these two US cases only as context for why the datasets are tainted; it states no holding, court, or date for either.

title: LAION-5B — CSAM; use Re-LAION-5B only
detail: CSAM was found in the original LAION-5B dataset (Thiel, Dec 2023) and it was taken down from hosting services; documented PII/medical-record leakage as well.
action: Use Re-LAION-5B (Aug 2024) only, and even then with a fresh safety scan; run PhotoDNA-equivalent hash matching on every image.
source: §13.4 (Thiel, Dec 2023); CSAM hash-matching mitigation in §18.2 and §17
note: Regime left null: the document grounds this in child-safety plus documented PII leakage rather than a named statute.

title: DataComp CommonPool — documented large-scale privacy problems
detail: DataComp CommonPool has documented large-scale privacy problems (arXiv:2506.17185) and substantial overlap with LAION-5B.
action: Avoid, or apply your own PII/CSAM filtering pipeline first.

title: WebVid-10M — withdrawn by its creators
detail: WebVid-10M was withdrawn by its creators.
action: Do not use.
note: The document does not state the reason for the withdrawal.

title: OpenSubtitles — copyrighted film/TV subtitles inside OPUS
detail: OpenSubtitles, distributed within OPUS, is copyrighted film/TV subtitle text.
action: Filter it explicitly out of any OPUS ingestion.
source: §13.4; also flagged in the §7 OPUS row
note: Note the tension the document itself surfaces: §A.4's conversational IndicTrans2 adaptation (arXiv:2606.29024) achieves its result using OpenSubtitles among its "only public data".

title: Alpaca-lineage data — OpenAI ToS provenance taint
detail: Alpaca, Bactrian-X, mAlpaca and many "self-instruct" sets were generated with OpenAI models, and OpenAI's ToS prohibits using outputs to train competing models. "Materially risky for a model that will compete with OpenAI."
action: Prefer Aya, Tülu 3, Nemotron, OpenThoughts, UPDESH instead.
source: §13.4; cross-referenced at §11.1 (Bactrian-X)

title: Reddit / Pushshift — licence or skip
detail: Reddit now licenses data commercially (~$203M disclosed contract value at IPO; ~$60M/yr Google, ~$70M/yr OpenAI reported). Free bulk scraping is against ToS and actively enforced.
action: Do not scrape. License or skip.
source: §13.4; deal figures repeated in §15.2 (all figures "reported", not confirmed by parties)

title: Twitter/X archives — ToS and active enforcement
detail: Twitter/X archives are covered by ToS restrictions with active enforcement.
action: Skip.

title: YouTube-derived corpora — ToS prohibits bulk download
detail: YouTube-Commons, YODAS, Panda-70M, InternVid and HD-VILA are YouTube-derived; YouTube ToS prohibits bulk download regardless of the underlying CC licence on individual videos.
action: Document a position or skip.
source: §13.4; also flagged in §9.2

title: Scraped Indian news — where the risk concentrates
detail: "The ANI v. OpenAI litigation exists precisely because of this." The Digital News Publishers Association and the Federation of Indian Publishers are intervenors. The legal position improved dramatically in July 2026, "but this is where the risk concentrates".
action: For Indian news, negotiate a retrieval/grounding deal rather than a training deal — cheaper, more readily accepted by publishers, and for a conversational model it delivers most of the value.
source: §13.4; the retrieval-not-training recommendation is from §15.3
note: §15.3 grounds that recommendation in the market shift to live-access deals (2 in 2023 → 11 in 2024 → 18 in 2025 → ~34 projected in 2026), with the Washington Post/OpenAI (April 2025) and Le Monde/Perplexity deals explicitly excluding training.

title: Identity documents — absolute blocklist
detail: Any government, personal or financial identity documents are barred under the DPDP Act "and also basic ethics".
action: Build automated Aadhaar/PAN/passport-pattern detectors into ingestion.
note: Same control as L20; recorded separately because §13.4 states it as a corpus-level prohibition rather than a pipeline requirement.

title: Internet Archive Indian book scans — item-level rights clearance
detail: The Internet Archive's Public Library of India / Digital Library of India holds ~500K+ scanned Indian books of mixed copyright status, many still in copyright. "Requires item-level rights clearance. Enormous prize, real risk."
action: Clear rights item by item before ingesting.
source: §10.2 clean curriculum sources table
note: Outside §§13–14, but recorded here because it is a licensing constraint of the same class. Related: §10.2 notes Shodhganga (INFLIBNET) Indian PhD theses retain author copyright per thesis.
